newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO poised to close Hebron deal this week.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO poised to close Hebron deal this week.

text.p: Israeli and Palestinian officials said on Monday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was poised to hand over the occupied West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian self-rule.

An aide to Yasser Arafat said the long-elusive deal to transfer 80 percent of Hebron would be signed at a summit on Tuesday between the Palestinian leader and Netanyahu if negotiators wrapped up unresolved issues on Monday night.
"Otherwise, negotiations will continue and the agreement will be signed either Thursday or Friday," Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters.
U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, who pushed and pulled the sides together on orders from President Bill Clinton, flew in from Washington on Monday to mediate any last-minute snags.
Ross met Netanyahu in Jerusalem soon after his arrival, and was to meet Arafat in Gaza later in the day.

"We expect to conclude today all the subjects...After signing, in a very short time redeployment will take place," Israel's Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said earlier when he joined talks with PLO officials.
Palestinian negotiator Mohammad Dahlan said a troop redeployment would take place within a week.

Opposed to swapping occupied land for peace, the 47-year-old Netanyahu ran an election campaign against the self-rule accords that Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres, his Nobel prize-winning predecessors, signed with the PLO starting in 1993.
But also vowing to uphold existing peace deals, Netanyahu ousted Peres in a May poll, albeit by fewer than 30,000 votes.

Hebron, long a flashpoint of violence between Arabs and Jews, is the last of seven West Bank towns scheduled for self-rule under an agreement signed in 1995. It was due to have been given self-rule nine months ago.

Security concerns held up the handover. Peres delayed it over a wave of Islamist suicide bombings in Israel that killed 59 people. Then talks got stuck on Netanyahu's demands for better protection for the 400 Jews in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs. Arafat also put forward demands.

Under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, Netanyahu stayed in the negotiations while emphasising that 20 percent of the town, including Hebron's Jews and the tomb of the biblical patriarch Abraham, would remain under Israeli control.

Many of Netanyahu's right-wing followers, including Jewish settlers, view the West Bank as the biblical birthright of Jews -- the Land of Israel promised them by God. Many view Arafat as a "terrorist" bent on Israel's destruction.

Underscoring tensions in Hebron, Israeli troops arrested several Palestinian construction workers on Monday after Jewish settlers complained they were doing work close to a Jewish enclave in the town, Palestinian witnesses said.

Senior PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said Israel and the PLO would discuss adding international observers from Turkey, Italy, Sweden and Switzerland to the Norwegian force making up the 200-strong Temporary International Presence in Hebron.
In parliament, Netanyahu's coalition handily defeated a motion of no confidence in the government proposed by the far-right Moledet party in protest at the Hebron deal.

But several coalition members, including members of Netanyahu's own cabinet, stayed away during the vote to show they opposed the agreement. Four of Netanyahu's 18 cabinet members say they will oppose the deal in a cabinet vote.
Defending the accord to Likud party colleagues, Netanyahu said the draft agreement contained at least 10 "significant changes" from that signed by Labour a year ago.

He said the changes make sure Hebron's Jews "will not be in range of (PLO) rifles, that we will have an armed military presence on the commanding hills, that the Jewish community will not be 'strangled' by dense (Arab) construction surrounding it."
But PLO officials said buffer zones in Hebron were still under discussion, as was Israeli army control of city heights.
